subject: history

questions.content: In which country did the Industrial Revolution begin, from around the 1760s?
questions.explanation: Britain was the first country to industrialise, beginning in the later eighteenth century with textiles, coal, iron and steam power.

questions.content: Which invention, developed by James Watt in the 1760s and 1770s, made steam engines far more efficient?
questions.explanation: Watt's separate condenser saved fuel compared with Newcomen's engine, making steam power practical for factories and mines.

questions.content: Which natural resource was most important as fuel for steam engines and for smelting iron?
questions.explanation: Britain had large, accessible coal deposits, which powered engines and, as coke, smelted iron.

questions.content: What was the main purpose of the 'Agricultural Revolution' changes such as crop rotation and the seed drill?
options: To reduce the size of farms to nothing
To ban the use of horses
To grow more food with fewer workers
questions.explanation: Better farming produced more food and freed labour, so people could move to towns and work in industry.

questions.content: Which of these was a famous early railway line opened in 1830, carrying both goods and passengers using steam locomotives?
questions.explanation: The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened in 1830 and was the first inter-city line run entirely by steam locomotives to a timetable.

questions.content: An invented region, Calderdale, had fast rivers, coal and iron deposits near the surface, a growing population and wealthy merchants looking for places to invest. Why would these features help it industrialise?
options: They offered power, raw materials, workers and capital
questions.explanation: Industrialisation needs power, materials, labour and money to invest. Calderdale has all four.

questions.content: Why did the invention of the spinning jenny, water frame and mule affect the textile industry so strongly?
options: They made weaving by hand compulsory
They allowed far more thread to be spun, moving textile production into factories
They banned the import of cotton
questions.explanation: Spinning machines multiplied the output of thread per worker. Water frames and mules needed power and space, so work moved into factories.

questions.content: A student says, 'Britain industrialised first only because it had coal.' Which statement is the best response?
options: Coal mattered, but so did capital, empire and trade markets, stable government, a growing workforce and transport links
Correct, since other countries had no coal
questions.explanation: Strong causation answers combine several linked factors. Other countries such as Belgium also had coal, so coal alone does not explain Britain's lead.

questions.content: How did canals and later railways help the Industrial Revolution?
options: They cut the cost and time of moving coal, raw materials and finished goods
They stopped people moving to towns
questions.explanation: Cheap, quick transport linked mines, factories and markets, allowing larger-scale production.

questions.content: Read this invented advert from 1790: 'Hallam's Mill offers 300 spindles worked by a single water wheel. One operator can now do the work of twenty hand-spinners.' What does this extract best illustrate?
options: The effect of mechanisation on productivity
questions.explanation: The claim that one operator can do the work of twenty shows how machines increased output per worker. As an advert, its figure may be exaggerated.

questions.content: Abraham Darby's use of coke instead of charcoal to smelt iron from 1709 was important because
options: it was only used for jewellery
it reduced the use of coal
it allowed cheaper, larger-scale production of iron without relying on scarce wood
questions.explanation: Coke made it possible to produce iron in greater quantity, which later supplied machines, bridges and railways.

questions.content: Why did enclosure of common land contribute to the Industrial Revolution?
options: It gave every villager a bigger farm
It made larger, more efficient farms, and many landless labourers moved to find work in towns
It increased the number of village fairs
questions.explanation: Enclosure allowed landowners to farm more efficiently. It also removed many people's access to common land, adding to the supply of workers for new industries.

questions.content: A historian argues that the availability of capital was as important as any invention. Which evidence would best support this?
options: Wealthy merchants, banks and landowners invested money in canals, mills and mines, and so inventions could be built at scale
questions.explanation: Inventions need investment to become working industries. Profits from trade and farming supplied this money.

questions.content: Which statement best explains why the first Industrial Revolution is described as a 'revolution' even though it took decades?
options: It happened in a single year
It was started by a war
It transformed how goods were made, where people lived and worked, and the structure of society, within a few generations
questions.explanation: 'Revolution' refers to the scale of change compared to earlier history, not to the speed of any single event.

questions.content: An invented country, Veldmark, has plenty of coal and a growing population, but its rulers ban banks from lending to private businesses and tax trade heavily. Which prediction about Veldmark's industrial growth is best supported?
options: It will industrialise as fast as Britain regardless
It will probably industrialise more slowly, as access to capital and trade is restricted
It will not have any industry as it has coal
questions.explanation: Natural resources are only one condition. Without investment and free trade, industries find it harder to grow.

questions.content: Which line of reasoning best shows how the Agricultural and Industrial Revolutions were LINKED?
options: They were unrelated and happened in different centuries
Higher food output supported a growing population and released workers, while profits from farming gave investors money for industry
questions.explanation: Food, labour and capital flowed from farming to industry. The links between causes are what high-level answers should show.

questions.content: The cotton industry of Lancashire relied on raw cotton from plantations in the Americas that used enslaved labour. What does this show about the causes of Britain's industrial growth?
options: Industrialisation depended only on British inventors
Britain's industrial growth was connected to wider imperial trade and exploitation, not only to events within Britain
Cotton was grown locally in Lancashire
Empire was not involved in industry
questions.explanation: Raw cotton imports and colonial markets were important for textile industries. Many historians therefore stress global links alongside domestic factors.

questions.content: Which comparison of the steam engine and water power best explains why steam helped factories spread?
options: Steam engines could be placed anywhere that had coal and water supplies, freeing factories from fast rivers
Steam power was invented before the wheel
questions.explanation: Water wheels tied mills to rivers. Steam engines allowed factories to be located in towns near workers, coal and transport.

note:
## What was the Industrial Revolution?
The **Industrial Revolution** was the shift from hand-made goods and farming to machine production, factories and towns. It began in Britain from around the 1760s and later spread to Belgium, the USA, Germany and beyond. Within a few generations it changed how people worked, where they lived and how wealth was made.

## Why Britain first? A set of linked causes
- **Agricultural change**: new methods such as crop rotation and the seed drill, along with enclosure of land, raised food output. A growing population could be fed and many people left the land to find work.
- **Natural resources**: Britain had coal and iron ore close to the surface and near rivers and ports.
- **Capital**: profits from trade, farming and the empire gave wealthy people money to invest in mills, canals and mines. Banks lent money.
- **Trade and empire**: colonies supplied raw materials such as cotton and offered markets for finished goods.
- **Transport**: rivers, coastal shipping, then canals and later railways moved heavy goods cheaply.
- **Stable government and ideas**: a relatively stable political system, protection of property and a culture that encouraged invention and science.
- **Population growth**: more workers and more customers.
No single cause is enough. Belgium and others also had coal, so you must show how causes combine.

## Key inventions to know
- **Textiles**: Kay's flying shuttle (1733), Hargreaves' spinning jenny (about 1764), Arkwright's water frame (1769), Crompton's mule (1779) and Cartwright's power loom (1785). Spinning and weaving moved from homes to factories.
- **Steam**: Newcomen's engine (1712) pumped water from mines. Watt's separate condenser (patented 1769) made engines far more efficient.
- **Iron**: Abraham Darby used coke to smelt iron from 1709. The Iron Bridge (1779) showed what iron could do.
- **Transport**: canals such as the Bridgewater Canal (1761), then railways. The Stockton and Darlington Railway opened in 1825 and the Liverpool and Manchester Railway in 1830. Stephenson's Rocket won the Rainhill trials in 1829.

## Why did factories develop?
Machines were big, costly and needed power. It made sense to bring workers and machines together in one place. At first water wheels set mills beside rivers. Steam power later allowed factories to be built in towns.

## Worked example
Question: 'Explain why steam power was important to industrial growth.' Answer: Steam engines could pump water from deep mines, so more coal was dug. The coal then fuelled more engines. Because engines did not depend on rivers, factories could be located close to workers and transport. This led to growth of towns such as Manchester. So steam power created a cycle of growth.

## Common mistakes
- Giving a single reason for Britain's lead.
- Mixing up inventors and machines, or giving a date with no explanation of why it mattered.
- Saying the Industrial Revolution happened overnight.
- Ignoring the global links of trade and empire.

## How this is examined
You may see a short source, such as an invented advert or report, and be asked to state what it shows, explain a cause, or discuss which factors were most important. Higher-level answers link causes together and rank them with reasons.

Exam tip: When you name an invention, always add what it changed. 'The water frame, because it moved spinning into factories' earns more than the name and date alone.

flashcards.back: The shift from hand production and farming to machines, factories and towns, beginning in Britain from the 1760s.
Food surplus, coal and iron, capital, trade and empire, good transport, stable government and a growing population.
Improved the steam engine with a separate condenser (patented 1769), making it efficient enough for factories and mines.
Flying shuttle (1733), spinning jenny (about 1764), water frame (1769), mule (1779) and power loom (1785).
Used coke instead of charcoal to smelt iron from 1709, allowing cheaper, larger-scale iron production.
Fencing off common land into private farms. Farming became more efficient but many labourers lost access to land and moved to find work.
Stockton and Darlington (1825) and Liverpool and Manchester (1830), the first inter-city line run entirely by steam locomotives.

flashcards.front: Why did factories replace home working?
flashcards.back: Machines were costly, large and needed power, so it was efficient to gather workers and machines in one place.
It freed factories from river sites, pumped mines to produce more coal and powered machines and locomotives.

subject: history

questions.content: What is URBANISATION?
options: The growth of towns and cities as more people live there
questions.explanation: Urbanisation is the movement of people into towns and cities, which happened rapidly in industrial Britain.

questions.content: Which disease spread through dirty water and killed thousands in British towns in the 1830s and 1840s?
questions.explanation: Cholera outbreaks, for example in 1832 and 1848-49, were linked to contaminated water and poor sanitation in crowded towns.

questions.content: In the new factories, who often worked long hours for low pay, including many children?
questions.explanation: Working-class families depended on wages. Children were cheap and could work close to machinery.

questions.content: Which word describes the new social group of wealthy factory owners, merchants and professionals who grew in influence?
questions.explanation: The middle class, including industrialists and professionals, expanded as industry grew, and they pressed for more political power.

questions.content: The working week in an early factory was usually
options: very long, often twelve hours or more a day, six days a week
questions.explanation: Before reforms, factory hours were long and set by owners. Machines kept to the pace of the engine, not the worker.

questions.content: Read this invented extract from a doctor's notebook, 1842: 'In the courts off Mill Lane, forty families share a single pump and two privies. Most rooms hold a whole family. Fever is constant.' What does it best illustrate?
options: Poor housing and sanitation in rapidly growing industrial towns
The success of the Public Health Act
questions.explanation: Shared water supplies and overcrowded rooms were typical of poor working-class districts, and spread disease.

questions.content: Why was child labour valued by many factory owners?
options: Children could not be hurt by machines
Children were cheap, could be paid less and were small enough to work in tight spaces
Children had been trained for years
questions.explanation: Employers saved money by paying children low wages. Their small size suited tasks such as crawling under machines or in narrow mine passages.

questions.content: Which of these is an ECONOMIC change linked to the Industrial Revolution?
options: A growth in mass production and a rise in trade and national wealth
A reduction in the use of money
questions.explanation: Factories produced goods in large quantities and cheaply, boosting trade and overall wealth. But not everyone shared in this wealth equally.

questions.content: An invented table of average living standards in two towns gives: Town A, life expectancy 36 years, built in the 1700s with wide streets; Town B, life expectancy 26 years, a factory town that expanded fast in the 1830s. Which statement is best supported?
options: Factory towns always had longer lives
Life expectancy depends only on the date of building
Fast, unplanned growth and poor sanitation probably contributed to the lower life expectancy in Town B
The data proves factories cause illness everywhere
questions.explanation: The evidence suggests a link but does not prove one cause. Fast growth with poor sanitation was a recognised risk. Other factors could also matter.

questions.content: Which statement best describes the effect of industrialisation on the gap between rich and poor?
options: It created great wealth for some factory owners while many workers lived in poor, crowded conditions, at least at first
It had no effect on wealth
questions.explanation: Historians generally agree that national wealth increased but many workers saw little improvement in the early decades, with living standards improving more clearly later.

questions.content: A historian argues that the Industrial Revolution made life better for ordinary people in the long run. Which piece of evidence best supports the claim?
options: Child labour in mills in the 1810s
Rising real wages, cheaper clothing and improved public health in the later nineteenth century
questions.explanation: Long-run improvement is shown by later gains in wages, goods and health. The other options are early negative effects.

questions.content: What was a main effect of factory work on the daily routine of workers compared with farm work?
options: Work was timed by clocks and bells and workers could be fined for lateness
questions.explanation: Factory discipline imposed fixed hours and rules. This was a major change from the seasonal rhythm of farm work.

questions.content: Why did many working families in the early 1800s send children to work rather than to school?
options: Family wages were low, children's earnings were needed, and there was no national system of compulsory schooling until later in the century
questions.explanation: Poverty pushed families to rely on every wage. Compulsory elementary schooling came only after the Education Act of 1870 and later laws.

questions.content: Consider two claims about the early Industrial Revolution. Claim 1: 'Living standards fell.' Claim 2: 'Living standards rose.' Why might historians disagree?
options: They use different measures, such as wages, health, working hours and housing, and different groups and time periods
One group of historians invented the factories
There is no evidence at all
Everyone had exactly the same experience
questions.explanation: Different measures and groups give different results. Skilled workers might gain while handloom weavers or crowded town families suffered. Good answers acknowledge this complexity.

questions.content: Handloom weavers in the early 1800s often saw their incomes fall when power looms spread. What does this show?
options: Industrial change created winners and losers, and some skilled workers lost out
questions.explanation: New machines made some skills less valuable and caused unemployment or lower wages for those workers, while other groups gained.

questions.content: Which line of reasoning best explains why the growth of cities created new social tensions?
options: Crowding, differences in wealth and a lack of political voice for workers produced anger and demands for change
Cities were built after tensions ended
questions.explanation: Urban crowding, inequality and exclusion from voting led to protest movements such as Chartism and calls for reform.

questions.content: A student says, 'The Industrial Revolution was a disaster for women.' Which response shows the most balanced evaluation?
options: Disagree, women lived better in every way
Women gained wages and some independence in factories, but worked long hours for lower pay than men, and often combined paid work with housework
questions.explanation: A balanced view includes both opportunities and disadvantages. Women's wages were typically lower and their burden was often double.

questions.content: An invented source, a 1845 pamphlet written by a mill owner, says: 'Wages in my mills are the highest in the county and my workers are content.' A second source, a worker's petition from the same mill in 1845, lists fines, long hours and unsafe machines. What is the best conclusion?
options: The owner must be right as he pays wages
The workers must be right as they are poor
The sources conflict because each has an interest, so a historian should look for further evidence such as inspector reports and wage books
questions.explanation: Both have a motive. Cross-checking with independent evidence such as official records allows a more reliable judgement.

note:
## The big picture
Industrialisation changed Britain's economy and society. Wealth and production soared, but the speed of change brought problems. Historians still debate whether ordinary people were better or worse off in the early decades. A good answer shows that effects were different for different groups and times.

## Economic change
- **Mass production**: factories made goods faster and cheaper.
- **Growth in trade**: exports of textiles and iron goods grew, and Britain became a leading trading nation.
- **New industries and jobs**: coal, iron, engineering, railways and shipbuilding.
- **Decline of some old trades**: handloom weavers saw their incomes fall as power looms spread.
- **Capitalism**: owners invested money to earn profit, and workers sold their labour for wages.

## Social change
- **Urbanisation**: towns such as Manchester, Leeds, Birmingham and Glasgow grew very rapidly as people moved from the countryside.
- **Housing and health**: much working-class housing was cheap, crowded and badly built. Many families shared pumps and toilets. Water-borne diseases such as cholera and typhoid spread. Cholera outbreaks occurred in 1832, 1848-49 and 1854.
- **Work**: factory work followed the clock and the machine. Days of twelve hours or more were common. Fines and strict discipline were used.
- **Children and women**: employers used cheap labour of children and women. Children worked in mills and in mines, where small bodies could reach narrow spaces. Many women were paid less than men.
- **New classes**: a wealthy middle class of factory owners, merchants and professionals grew in importance. The industrial working class grew in size but had little political voice.

## Was it good or bad?
Evidence for improvement: more goods at lower prices, new jobs, higher national wealth and, later in the nineteenth century, better wages and health. Evidence against: dangerous work, child labour, pollution, overcrowding and disease, especially in the early decades. Some groups, such as skilled engineers, gained, while others, such as handloom weavers, lost out. Your answer should name groups and timescales.

## Worked example
Question: 'Explain one way in which industrialisation harmed working people.' Answer: Rapid urban growth meant that many families lived in overcrowded courts without clean water or proper drains. This allowed diseases such as cholera to spread quickly, as in 1832 and 1848-49. So the growth of industry led to poor health, especially among poor town dwellers.

## Common mistakes
- Writing that everyone suffered or everyone benefited.
- Describing conditions without explaining why they arose.
- Forgetting that improvements took decades.
- Listing facts without linking them to a question.

## How this is examined
Questions often give an extract such as a doctor's notes, a worker's petition or a table of data about towns. You may be asked to state what the source shows, to explain a cause of the conditions, or to evaluate whether industrialisation improved lives. Remember to consider the origin and purpose of each source.

Exam tip: Use 'but' and 'however' to show both sides, and finish by judging which side is stronger and why.

flashcards.back: The growth of towns and cities as people move from the countryside, as in industrial Britain from the late 1700s.
A water-borne disease that spread in crowded British towns with poor sanitation, with major outbreaks in 1832, 1848-49 and 1854.
Children were cheap, could be controlled easily and were small enough for narrow spaces in mills and mines.
A growing group of factory owners, merchants and professionals who gained wealth and wanted more political influence.
Long hours, low pay, strict discipline, fines and dangerous machinery, with little protection.
Industrial change helped some groups, such as owners and skilled engineers, but hurt others, such as handloom weavers.
Women gained wages but were paid less than men and often had housework as well as factory work.
Cheaper goods, higher national wealth and, later in the nineteenth century, rising real wages and better public health.
An economic system in which owners invest money to make profit and workers sell their labour for wages.

subject: history

questions.content: What did the Factory Act of 1833 do?
options: Banned children under 9 from working in textile mills and set up factory inspectors
questions.explanation: The 1833 Act banned employment of children under nine in textile factories, limited hours for older children and created paid inspectors to enforce the law.

questions.content: Who were the Luddites?
options: Workers who smashed machines that threatened their jobs, around 1811-1816
questions.explanation: Luddites were textile workers who attacked machines in protest at falling wages and job losses, notably in 1811-1816.

questions.content: What was a TRADE UNION?
options: An organisation of workers who join together to improve pay and conditions
questions.explanation: Trade unions allow workers to bargain collectively with employers.

questions.content: Chartism, from 1838, mainly campaigned for
options: political rights for working men, including a vote for all men and a secret ballot
questions.explanation: The People's Charter of 1838 had six points, including votes for all men and voting by secret ballot.

questions.content: Edwin Chadwick's 1842 report is best known for
options: linking filth and poor sanitation to disease and calling for clean water and drains
questions.explanation: Chadwick's report on the sanitary condition of the working population argued that disease was linked to dirty conditions and called for public sanitation. It helped lead to the Public Health Act of 1848.

questions.content: Read this invented petition, 1832: 'We, the workers of Barrowfield Mill, ask Parliament to limit our children's hours to ten a day, for they fall asleep at the looms and many are crippled.' What was the most likely purpose of the petition?
options: To persuade lawmakers to reform working conditions
questions.explanation: A petition is a request for action. This one aims to persuade Parliament to pass limits on child working hours.

questions.content: Why were early factory reforms often hard to enforce?
options: The laws applied only to farms
Too few inspectors, and many owners and parents ignored or evaded the rules
questions.explanation: Enforcement needed inspectors. The 1833 Act created only a handful, and owners sometimes falsified ages while families depended on children's wages.

questions.content: The Mines Act of 1842 is important because it
options: banned women and boys under ten from working underground
questions.explanation: A report on child labour in mines shocked the public, and the 1842 Act banned women and boys under ten from underground work.

questions.content: Why did some employers and politicians oppose factory reform?
options: They believed government should not interfere with business and that regulation raised costs
They wanted children to go to school
They had never seen a factory
questions.explanation: Many supported 'laissez-faire', the idea that the state should not interfere in the economy. Others argued that reform harmed profits and families' incomes.

questions.content: Robert Owen's mill at New Lanark in Scotland is often cited as an example of
options: a factory with the worst conditions
an employer improving conditions, with better housing, schools and shorter hours for children
questions.explanation: Owen, a mill owner, provided schooling and better housing while running a profitable mill, and argued that good treatment of workers was possible.

questions.content: In 1834 six farm labourers in Tolpuddle, Dorset, were sentenced to transportation to Australia for
options: setting up a union and swearing an oath
questions.explanation: The Tolpuddle Martyrs formed a friendly society or union and were convicted for taking an illegal oath. A public campaign led to their pardon.

questions.content: The Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834 set up workhouses where conditions were deliberately harsh. What was the reasoning behind this?
options: To encourage the poor to enjoy the workhouse
To make relief unattractive so that only truly desperate people would apply, saving money
questions.explanation: The 'less eligibility' principle held that conditions inside should be worse than those of the poorest labourer outside, discouraging claims and cutting costs.

questions.content: Which factor best explains why the Factory Act of 1847 (the Ten Hours Act) succeeded after earlier attempts had weaker results?
options: Years of campaigning by reformers such as Lord Shaftesbury, public reports and pressure from workers had changed opinion
questions.explanation: Long campaigns, evidence from official inquiries and growing political pressure created conditions for change. Reform was usually a slow, step-by-step process.

questions.content: A student argues that the 1832 Reform Act did little for the working class. Which evidence best supports the claim?
options: It extended the vote mainly to middle-class property owners, while working men remained without the vote
questions.explanation: The Act gave seats to new industrial towns and widened the vote, but the qualification was based on property, so most working men could not vote.

questions.content: Compare the Luddites and the Chartists. Which statement is the most accurate?
options: Both campaigned to give women the vote
Luddites used petitions only, Chartists broke machines
Luddites mostly attacked machinery as a protest about jobs and wages, while Chartists campaigned for political change such as votes for working men
questions.explanation: Luddites responded directly to the economic effect of machines, whereas Chartists sought a political solution. Both show worker discontent.

questions.content: Which factor made public health reform increasingly likely in the 1840s and 1850s?
options: Cholera spread beyond poor districts and threatened the wealthy as well, while reports such as Chadwick's provided evidence
questions.explanation: Disease affected all classes, so the middle class had a self-interest in reform. Studies like John Snow's work on the 1854 Broad Street pump also showed the water link.

questions.content: An invented historian argues that factory reform came mainly from 'the generosity of kind owners'. Which counter-argument is strongest?
options: Reform needed pressure from workers' campaigns, investigations and laws, and many owners opposed it, so generosity alone does not explain it
questions.explanation: A few reforming employers such as Owen existed, but most change was achieved through campaigns, official inquiries and Parliament, often against owners' wishes.

questions.content: Which statement best evaluates how effective the early reforms were?
options: They solved all problems at once
They gradually improved conditions in some areas, but were limited by weak enforcement and by what governments were willing to regulate
questions.explanation: A balanced view recognises progress, such as limits on child labour and public health acts, alongside gaps in enforcement and coverage. Reforms accumulated over decades.

note:
## Why did reform happen?
Industrialisation created wealth but also dangerous work, child labour, overcrowded towns and disease. Over the nineteenth century, pressure from workers, campaigners, journalists and some politicians pushed governments to act. At first governments held to a policy of **laissez-faire**, the idea that the state should not interfere with business. Evidence of suffering gradually changed minds.

## Worker responses
- **Luddites (1811-1816)**: textile workers who broke machines in protest at lost jobs and falling wages. The government made machine-breaking a very serious crime.
- **Trade unions**: workers joined together to bargain. The Combination Acts, which banned unions, were repealed in 1824. In 1834 the Tolpuddle Martyrs were transported for forming a union and taking an oath. A public campaign led to their pardon.
- **Chartism (from 1838)**: a mass movement for political rights. The People's Charter had six points, including a vote for all men and a secret ballot. Parliament rejected the petitions, but most of the points were later achieved.
- **Co-operatives**: the Rochdale Pioneers (1844) formed a shop owned by its members.

## Factory and mine reform
- **1833 Factory Act**: no children under nine in textile mills, limited hours for children, and factory inspectors to enforce it.
- **1842 Mines Act**: banned women and boys under ten from working underground, after a shocking report.
- **1847 Ten Hours Act**: limited the hours of women and young people in textile factories.
Reformers included Lord Shaftesbury, who campaigned for years. Laws were hard to enforce, as there were few inspectors and some owners falsified ages.

## Public health reform
Edwin Chadwick's 1842 report linked disease to filth and bad drainage. The **Public Health Act of 1848** set up a central board and allowed towns to create local health boards. Cholera in 1848-49 and 1854 increased pressure, and John Snow's work in 1854 showed that cholera in Soho was linked to a water pump. The **Public Health Act of 1875** made many sanitary measures compulsory.

## Political reform
The **1832 Reform Act** gave seats to new industrial towns and widened the vote, but mainly to property-owning middle-class men. Workers wanted more, which fed Chartism. Later acts extended the vote further.

## Other responses
The **Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834** introduced workhouses to cut the cost of relief. Reforming employers such as **Robert Owen** at New Lanark offered schools and better housing. Writers such as Friedrich Engels (1845) and Karl Marx and Engels (the Communist Manifesto, 1848) criticised capitalism.

## Worked example
Question: 'Explain why the Factory Act of 1833 did not end child labour.' Answer: The Act applied only to textile mills, and there were very few inspectors. Many parents relied on children's wages and some owners falsified ages. So it improved matters but its effects were limited.

## Common mistakes
- Mixing up the dates and content of different Acts.
- Saying one law solved everything.
- Forgetting that workers themselves campaigned.

## How this is examined
Expect a source such as a petition, a report or a speech and questions about its purpose, value and limitations, or a causation question such as 'Explain why reforms were introduced'. Higher marks need links between causes and a judgement on how effective reform was.

Exam tip: For 'how effective' questions, give one success and one limitation, then judge.

flashcards.back: The belief that governments should not interfere in business or the economy. It slowed early factory reform.
Textile workers who smashed machines around 1811-1816 in protest at job losses and falling wages.
A working-class movement from 1838 demanding political rights in the six-point People's Charter, including votes for all men.
Banned children under nine from textile mills, limited hours for older children and created factory inspectors.
Banned women and boys under ten from working underground, after a report exposed conditions in mines.
Limited the working day for women and young people in textile factories to ten hours.
His 1842 report linked disease to filth and poor drainage and led to the Public Health Act of 1848.
Gave seats to new industrial towns and widened the vote, mainly to middle-class property owners; most workers still had no vote.
Set up harsh workhouses so that relief would be unattractive and cheaper for taxpayers.
